analysis.one_liner: Imposes anti-fraud rules on mortgage servicers and mortgage-backed securities after the foreclosure crisis.
analysis.headline: The Foreclosure Fraud and Homeowner Abuse Prevention Act never got a single vote: referred to the Senate Banking Committee in April 2011, it sat there until the 112th Congress ended with no committee action, no floor debate, and no roll call.
analysis.plain_summary: In the wake of the foreclosure crisis and the "robo-signing" scandal, when banks were found signing foreclosure paperwork without verifying it, Senator Sherrod Brown proposed a bill targeting mortgage servicers — the companies that collect payments and handle foreclosures for investors. The bill would have brought mortgage-backed securities and their servicers under the Trust Indenture Act, directed the SEC to write rules for mortgage-related securities, capped the cost of force-placed insurance (expensive insurance a servicer buys on a homeowner's behalf and bills to them), imposed capital reserve standards on regulated lenders, and let borrowers sue servicers under the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act. It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee on April 14, 2011 and the committee never took it up. No other action was ever recorded before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners — especially those in default or facing foreclosure — gain new ways to challenge abusive servicing: the right to sue servicers in court, protection from being overcharged for force-placed insurance, and federal rules requiring fraud-prevention and capital reserves at the institutions handling their loans. Investors in mortgage-backed securities also gain, since servicers would become legally accountable under securities law.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Homeowners facing foreclosure and abusive servicing

how_it_helps.text: The bill brings mortgage-backed securities and the companies that service them under the Trust Indenture Act of 1939, making servicers legally accountable under securities law for the first time.
It directs the SEC to write requirements governing mortgage-related securities, adding federal oversight of the instruments at the center of the housing collapse.
It limits force-placed insurance charges: when a servicer buys insurance on a homeowner's behalf and bills the homeowner, the costs are capped at those of a standard homeowner's insurance policy.

It amends the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act so that securitized residential mortgage loans and their servicers are covered, and a debt collector who violates the Act in connection with such a debt faces civil liability — giving borrowers a private right of action against abusive servicers.
It directs federal banking regulators to set capital reserve standards, requiring lenders to hold reserves against losses.

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage servicers and the large banks that dominate servicing bear the cost: new SEC and banking regulations, capital reserve requirements, liability for collections abuses, and a cap on the profit margin in force-placed insurance. Issuers of mortgage-backed securities face stricter securities-law obligations. In principle some compliance costs could be passed on to borrowers through fees, and tighter lending standards can make credit slightly harder to get.
analysis.who_pays_short: Mortgage servicers, big banks, and MBS issuers

drawbacks.text: The bill adds a new layer of federal rulemaking — SEC requirements for mortgage-related securities and capital reserve standards across regulators — which regulated banks argue raises compliance costs that can be passed to borrowers through fees or tighter credit.

Expanding civil liability under the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act to securitized mortgages invites litigation against servicers, which critics say could slow down loan workouts and foreclosures alike.
Capping force-placed insurance costs at standard policy prices reduces revenue for the insurers that write those policies, which could affect coverage availability for properties in default.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary homeowners the benefits are direct and concrete: a right to sue abusive servicers, a cap on inflated force-placed insurance bills, and fraud-prevention rules at a moment when servicing errors were pushing people out of their homes. The costs fall mainly on servicers, banks, and insurers in the form of compliance, reserves, and liability — the kind of costs the institutions targeted were, by the bill's premise, imposing on borrowers through sloppy and fraudulent practices. The main design risk is that new compliance costs get passed through to borrowers, and that liability rules generate litigation on top of relief.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up — no hearing, no markup, no vote — so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Sherrod Brown introduced the bill on April 14, 2011, in the aftermath of the foreclosure crisis.
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
That referral was the last recorded action: the committee never scheduled a markup or vote, and the bill never reached the Senate floor before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.
The bill drew only three cosponsors in the Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage servicers and the large banks behind them are better off, because none of the new servicing rules, securities-law obligations, capital requirements, or borrower lawsuit rights in the bill ever took effect. Homeowners in foreclosure got no additional protection from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Mortgage servicers and the big banks behind them

for.name: Sen. Sherrod Brown
for.role: Sponsor; introduced the bill and referred it to the Banking Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Foreclosure Fraud and Homeowner Abuse Prevention Act of 2011 on April 14, 2011.

against.name: Senate Banking Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill after its April 14, 2011 referral; the committee took no recorded action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so there is no roll-call record; all known support came from Democrats (the sponsor plus three cosponsors), and the bill never advanced far enough to test Republican positions.

industries.note: Servicers would face new fraud-prevention rules, capital reserve standards, SEC oversight, and civil liability to borrowers under the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act — costs that come directly out of the fees and foreclosure practices the bill targets.

MBS issuers and their servicers would be brought under the Trust Indenture Act and subject to new SEC requirements for mortgage-related securities, adding accountability for the instruments at the center of the housing collapse.

Force-placed insurance — policies servicers buy on a homeowner's behalf and bill to them, historically at steep markups — would be capped at the cost of a standard homeowner's policy, cutting the industry's margin on this business.
